::: {.pageinfo}
Builds on [post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd), whose recipe every entry reuses, and on [post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd) for the pitch ruler. Each instrument's equations are stated; where they come from, and how each spectrum is computed, is in folds you can skip. About 35 minutes with the demos. Written in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.
:::

[]{#orchestra}Struck or plucked and left to ring, most instruments sound at the frequencies of their own eigenvalues, wherever those fall: a little sharp of the whole-number lines on a piano, far off them on a kalimba or a glockenspiel, scattered between them on a drum. Bowed or blown, and on the theremin, the partials sit exactly on the lines. Below, one instrument from each of the five [Hornbostel–Sachs](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hornbostel-sachs) classes, which sort instruments by what makes the sound (strings, air, solid bodies, stretched skins, electric circuits),[^hs] plays Grieg;[^grieg] every voice is built from the spectra on this page.

```{=html}
<p><b>The cards, as text.</b> <i>Where the stems come from.</i> Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound (Hornbostel and Sachs, 1914; electrophones added later). One recipe turns each into its stems. (1) For small motions, Newton's law on a small piece of the instrument takes the form u<sub>tt</sub> = −Au: u is the instrument's shape, and the operator A turns a shape into minus the acceleration it causes. (2) A shape that the operator only stretches, AX = λX, swings at one frequency, f = √λ / 2π. (3) Left to ring, every motion is a sum of such shapes (for a bounded object without friction; post 2 proves it for the string, and the paragraph below gives the theorem for the others), so the list of the λ's, the spectrum of the operator, decides where the stems stand.</p>
<p><i>Electrophone, sine theremin.</i> Kirchhoff's law on a coil and a capacitor; operator A = 1/LC, a single number, like a mass on a spring; spectrum f = 1/(2π√(LC)). One stem: a pure tone. A real theremin runs two such circuits at radio frequencies, the hand changing C of one, and you hear the difference of their frequencies, with overtones.</p>
<p><i>Chordophone, piano.</i> Newton's law on a short piece of stiff steel wire; operator A = −c² d²/dx² + κ² d⁴/dx⁴, ends pinned; spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = n f<sub>0</sub> √(1 + Bn²). Just above the lines, more so as n grows: a note, slightly stretched.</p>
<p><i>Aerophone, clarinet.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of the air in the tube; operator A = −c² d²/dx² on pressure, closed at the reed and open at the far end; the tube's spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = (2n − 1) c / 4L. Blown, the air repeats one cycle, so the partials sit exactly on the lines; the tube's odd modes make the odd ones strong and the even ones weak: a hollow note.</p>
<p><i>Idiophone, glockenspiel.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of a steel bar; operator A = κ² d⁴/dx⁴, both ends free; spectrum from cos βL cosh βL = 1, ratios 1 : 2.76 : 5.40. Off the lines, but the overtones die fast: a bright, clean note.</p>
<p><i>Membranophones, bass drum and timpani.</i> Newton's law on a small patch of the drumhead; operator A = −c²Δ, rim held still; spectrum from J<sub>m</sub>(ka) = 0, ratios 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 …; the timpani's spectrum is measured, not derived. Bass drum: struck off centre, mostly round modes, off the lines and fading fast: a boom with no clear pitch. Timpani: the same skin; the air it drags along pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the stroke favours them and the round modes fade fast: a note.</p>
<p><i>Every sound in this video was built from pure tones at these spectra. No recordings, no samples.</i> Made in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.</p>
</details></div>
```

The reason, in one sentence: **a ringing instrument moves as a sum of its own modes, as the string does, so you hear its spectrum; a bowed or blown one is pushed into one repeating cycle, and a repeating cycle has only whole-number partials.**

## The same recipe {#recipe}

Every instrument below is a problem of the same shape as the string's: an equation, how the object is held (its [boundary conditions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#boundary-condition)), and how it starts or how the player drives it.

For the ones left to ring, [post 2's conclusion](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#decoupling) holds in the same form: every motion is a sum of the operator's [eigenfunctions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenfunction), each swinging at $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$. The reason is the string's: on a bounded object with a reasonable edge, each of these operators is [self-adjoint](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-adjoint) and $\geq 0$, and has a [compact resolvent](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#compact-resolvent), so its eigenfunctions form an [orthonormal basis](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#orthonormal).[^ch] One new thing can happen: a *drift*, a shape with $\lambda = 0$, which moves as $a + bt$ instead of swinging; drifts split off from the rest.

The kettledrum is the exception. It radiates sound into the unbounded air around it, which makes its problem non-self-adjoint and takes it outside this theorem, and its full air loading is beyond this page, so its ratios here are measured.[^benade] The air's added mass alone would not take it outside: the drums entry's toy model of the air stays inside.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The three names in the theorem <span class="needs">uses Hilbert spaces</span></summary>

A *Sturm–Liouville problem* is $-(p\,X')' + q\,X = \lambda\,w\,X$ on a bounded interval, with $p, w > 0$ and one condition at each end of the form $\alpha X + \beta X' = 0$; the string ($p = c^2$, $q = 0$, $w = 1$) and the tubes, open or closed at each end, are of this form, and its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, [*Methods of Mathematical Physics*, vol. 1](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/naturwissenschaften/methods-of-mathematical-physics-978-3-527-41447-5), Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI). For a bar, $(A + 1)^{-1}$ is an integral operator with a kernel continuous on $[0, L]^2$, the Green's operator, which is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators applies to it, and its eigenfunctions are $A$'s. For a drumhead, Rellich's theorem says that on a bounded region, every sequence of shapes that vanish on the rim and have $\iint u^2$ and $\iint |\nabla u|^2$ bounded has a subsequence converging in mean square; this makes $(A + 1)^{-1}$ compact (L. C. Evans, [*Partial Differential Equations*](https://bookstore.ams.org/GSM/19.R), 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, section 5.7). A drift occurs only when $A$ has the eigenvalue 0: on this page, for the glockenspiel bar.

</details>
:::

## Two kinds of entry {#two-kinds}

A *ringing* entry is struck or plucked, then left alone: it moves as a sum of its modes, each swinging at its own $f_n$ and fading at its own rate, so its partials sit wherever its spectrum falls.

A *self-sustained* entry is fed by the player for as long as the note lasts, by a bow, an air jet, a reed or an amplifier, through a push that depends on the motion itself, and not in proportion to it. Its motion settles into one repeating cycle, a [self-sustained oscillation](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-sustained). So it has two spectra. The *resonator's spectrum* is that of the part being driven, the string, the air column, the reed or the circuit: the eigenvalues of its operator, where it would ring if struck. The *sound's spectrum* is that of one repeating cycle at a playing frequency near a resonance, so its partials are exact whole-number multiples ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)); the drive's waveform and the [resonator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#resonator) (for the violin, also the body) decide which are strong.

In every demo the stems are the partials of the sound on the pitch ruler, taller when stronger; in ringing entries they shrink as each partial fades. The picture moves at the same frequencies, slowed down so that one swing of the lowest takes about a second, and enlarged; where its strengths differ from the stems', the caption says why. Each entry ends with which of post 2's [six conditions](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#conditions) the instrument breaks.

## A piano {#piano}

A piano note is clear, but its upper partials run slightly sharp of the whole-number lines, more so the higher they are. The reason is the steel: a piano wire is a string and a bar at once, tension pulling it straight and the steel resisting bending, which pushes back hardest on the finest shapes. Time starts when the hammer leaves the wire.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} - \kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_{xx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0, L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $c^2 = T/\mu$, tension over mass per length; $\kappa^2 = EI/\mu$, with $E$ steel's [Young's modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#youngs-modulus) and $I = \pi d^4/64$ the [second moment of area](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#second-moment) of a wire of diameter $d$. The ends are [pinned](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#pinned): held, free to pivot. The hammer's blow $v_0$ is concentrated near $x = L/8$.

Post 2's sines are the eigenfunctions again, with $\lambda_n = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4$, $k = n\pi/L$: same shapes, other numbers. So
$$
\begin{gathered}
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \\
f_0 = \frac{c}{2L}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}.
\end{gathered}
$$
The factor $\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}$ is the stiffness's share.[^fr12]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="piano">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A piano wire between two pins, swinging in its first twelve modes"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The piano note's partials, each a little sharp of its whole-number line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">Middle C, struck an eighth of the way along, where the 8th mode stands still, so in the model its stem is zero. Computed: the stem positions, with B = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, a rough value for a middle C wire. Modelled: each mode starts in proportion to its height under the hammer, with a roll-off for the felt. Illustrative: the fading times.</p>
</div></div>
```

This is why tuners stretch octaves. The second partial exceeds twice the fundamental by a factor of about $1 + 3B/2$, so an exact 2 : 1 octave [beats](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beats); tuners widen octaves, most at the keyboard's ends, a stretch Railsback measured.[^railsback] The player controls the hammer's speed (harder is louder and brighter, as the felt stiffens when squashed),[^russell] the key's release, which drops a felt damper on the wire, and the pedals; none of them moves a frequency ([A Piano](../a-piano/index.qmd)).

All six of post 2's conditions hold while the key is down. The damper breaks two: it is friction over a short stretch that, unlike post 2's light touch, reaches every mode, and it lands at one moment, so the problem changes in time.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives</span></summary>

Take the piece of wire between $x$ and $x + dx$, of mass $\mu\,dx$. Tension gives it the string's net force, $T\,u_{xx}\,dx$ for small slopes ([post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#newton)). Bending gives it the bar's: a bent wire carries the [bending moment](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#moment) $M = EI\,u_{xx}$, the turning balance of each thin slice makes the sideways *shear force* $V = -M_x$, and the shear forces on the two faces differ by $V_x\,dx = -EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx$ (the kalimba's fold below has the steps). Newton's law takes the total force, so the two add:
$$
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}.
$$
Small slopes also keep the tension at $T$. At each end the bridge or the bearing point holds the wire in place, $u = 0$, and if it lets the wire pivot freely it exerts no bending moment, $u_{xx} = 0$. The model takes a plain, uniform steel wire; bass strings are wound with copper, which adds mass but little stiffness (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 12).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses derivatives and square roots</span></summary>

$X = \sin kx$ with $k = n\pi/L$ vanishes at both ends, and so does $X'' = -k^2X$: both pinned conditions hold. Two derivatives multiply it by $-k^2$ and four by $k^4$, so $AX = (c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4)X$ with $A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$: the sines are eigenfunctions, and the string's eigenvalue and the bar's add. There are no others: the sines are already a basis (post 2's theorem), and $A$ is symmetric with these ends, so an eigenfunction for any other eigenvalue would be orthogonal to every sine, hence zero. Factoring, $\lambda_n = c^2k^2(1 + (EI/T)k^2)$, and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$ gives the formula with $B = \pi^2EI/TL^2$. For a middle C wire, roughly $d = 1$ mm and $L = 0.6$ m, steel's $E = 2\times10^{11}$ Pa and density 7850 kg/m³ need a tension of about 610 N, and then $B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}$: the 10th partial sits $1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37$ [cents](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#cents) sharp of ten times the fundamental. For the octave, $f_2/f_1 = 2\sqrt{(1 + 4B)/(1 + B)} \approx 2(1 + 3B/2)$. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.

</details>
:::

## A kalimba {#kalimba}

A kalimba tine gives a click, then a clean note. Its overtones sit far off the whole-number lines, but the first one, strong at the attack, dies within a fraction of a second, and leaves the fundamental.[^chapman] The tine is a steel bar clamped at the bridge and free at its tip, springing back because steel resists bending. The thumb pushes the tip aside a distance $h$ and lets go.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_x = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0, \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = \frac{h\,x^2(3L - x)}{2L^3}, \\ u_t(x, 0) = 0.
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$, with $\rho$ the density and $S$ the cross-section's area; the base is [clamped](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#clamped), unable to move or tilt, and the tip [free](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#free-end). The start is the smooth cubic a push at the tip bends the tine into; a corner would cost infinite bending energy $\int (u_{xx})^2$. It fails only $u_{xxx}(L) = 0$, where the thumb pushed, which post 2's [definition of a solution](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#decoupling) allows (fold).

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4$, where $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1$, so $\beta_nL = 1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, \dots$ and
$$
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\beta_n^2}{2\pi},
$$
in the ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, off the lines.[^fr2]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="kalimba">

  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The tine's partials at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest frequency, off the whole-number lines"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A tine at A4, 440 Hz, pushed at its tip and let go. Computed: the stem positions and each stem's starting height, the push on the bridge (the shear force at the clamp) from the cubic start. Illustrative: the fading times, chosen to match <a href="https://acoustics.org/pressroom/httpdocs/155th/chapman.htm">Chapman</a>'s observation that the overtones die within a fraction of a second; the stems shrink as each partial fades. The tine is drawn as it moves; in displacement its first overtone is only 2.5% of the fundamental, so the picture shows mostly the first mode, while in the push on the bridge it starts at 55%.</p>
</div></div>
```

The model gives where the overtones are and how strongly they start (in the push on the bridge, the first at 55% of the fundamental); how fast they fade is Chapman's measurement. Since $\beta_nL$ does not depend on $L$, $f_1 \propto 1/L^2$: half the length sounds two octaves up, and makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge.[^kmagic] The player sets the loudness by how far the tip is pushed, and can stop a tine with a finger.

All six of post 2's conditions hold in the model.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives and an integral over a cross-section</span></summary>

Bend the bar, and fibers on the outside of the curve stretch while those on the inside compress; a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length. For small slopes the curvature is $u_{xx}$, and a fiber at height $y$ above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction $-y\,u_{xx}$, so by Hooke's law it carries the force per unit area $-E\,y\,u_{xx}$. Over the cross-section these forces cancel, but their turning effects add up to the [bending moment](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#moment)
$$
\begin{gathered}
M = -\int y\,(-E\,y\,u_{xx})\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \\
I = \int y^2\,dA .
\end{gathered}
$$
Each face of a thin slice also carries a sideways shear force $V$. A thin slice's rotational inertia is negligible, so the turning effects on it balance: $V\,dx + dM = 0$, that is, $V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx}$. The shear forces on the two faces differ by $V_x\,dx$, which accelerates the slice's mass $\rho S\,dx$:
$$
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx},
$$
the [Euler–Bernoulli beam](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beam) equation, with $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$. A fourth-order equation needs two conditions at each end. The clamped base can neither move nor tilt: $u = u_x = 0$. At the free tip nothing bends or pushes the bar: $M = 0$ and $V = 0$, that is, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. The model ignores the slices' rotational inertia and shear deformation, which matter only for thick bars and high modes (Wikipedia, [Euler–Bernoulli beam theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Bernoulli_beam_theory)).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses a 2×2 determinant</span></summary>

With $\lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4$ the mode equation is $X'''' = \beta^4X$, solved by $\cos\beta x$, $\sin\beta x$, $\cosh\beta x$ and $\sinh\beta x$, where $\cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2$ and $\sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2$ are the [hyperbolic functions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hyperbolic). The clamp, $X(0) = X'(0) = 0$, leaves
$$
\begin{aligned}
X = {} & a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
& + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x).
\end{aligned}
$$
With $c_1 = \cos\beta L$, $s_1 = \sin\beta L$, $c_2 = \cosh\beta L$, $s_2 = \sinh\beta L$, the free tip's $X''(L) = X'''(L) = 0$ reads $-(c_1 + c_2)a - (s_1 + s_2)b = 0$ and $(s_1 - s_2)a - (c_1 + c_2)b = 0$. A solution other than $a = b = 0$ exists exactly when the [determinant](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#determinant) vanishes:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
& \quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
\end{aligned}
$$
using $c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1$ and $c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1$. So $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1$. Since $\cosh\beta L$ grows fast, $\cos\beta L$ must be near 0, so $\beta_nL$ is near $(n - \tfrac12)\pi$; numerically $1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, 10.9955$. Pinned ends would give the sines and the ratios $1 : 4 : 9$; the clamp and the free tip shift the first root most, which puts the ratios off the lines.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The cubic start, and how much of each mode it holds <span class="needs">uses integration by parts</span></summary>

Before release, a push $F$ at the tip holds the tine still. Inside, nothing pushes, so $EI\,u_0'''' = 0$: $u_0$ is a cubic. The clamp gives $u_0(0) = u_0'(0) = 0$, the free tip carries no moment, $u_0''(L) = 0$, and the tip height is $h$: this leaves $u_0 = h\,x^2(3L - x)/2L^3$, smooth, with $u_0'''(L) = -3h/L^3 \neq 0$, the shear force $F = 3EIh/L^3$ of the thumb. Any shape with a corner has $u_x$ jumping, so $u_{xx}$ contains a spike and the bending energy $\tfrac12 EI\int(u_{xx})^2$ is infinite; a finite push cannot store infinite energy. In post 2's definition a solution is tested only against smooth shapes $\varphi$ in the operator's domain, through $\langle u(t), \varphi\rangle$, so the series of post 2 needs only a start of finite bending energy with $u_0 = u_0' = 0$ at the clamp; the tip's natural conditions need not hold. Its coordinates: with the modes $X_n$ scaled so that $\int_0^L X_n^2 = L$, integrating by parts four times gives $\rho SL\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L)$, and $X_n(L) = \pm 2$ for every $n$, so $a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2$ and $a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%$. The bridge feels the shear force at the clamp, $EI\,u_{xxx}(0)$, in which mode $n$ carries the extra factor $X_n'''(0) \propto \sigma_n\beta_n^3$ ($\sigma_1 = 0.734$, $\sigma_2 = 1.018$): there the second mode starts at about 55% of the first. Chapman measured one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental on a real kalimba, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack (D. M. F. Chapman, [The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba)](https://acoustics.org/pressroom/httpdocs/155th/chapman.htm), Acoustics'08 Paris, 2008).

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the kalimba →](kalimba.qmd)**

## A glockenspiel {#glockenspiel}

A glockenspiel gives a bright, clear note although its overtones sit off the lines: they are high and die quickly, leaving the fundamental.[^scavone] Its bar is the same kind of steel bar as the kalimba's tine, with both ends free; it rests on soft supports and is struck with a mallet.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$ as for the kalimba, and $v_0$ is the mallet's blow, concentrated where it lands.

Two eigenvalues are 0: the bar sliding ($X = 1$) or tilting ($X = x$) without bending, two drifts, which make no sound. The others are $\lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4$ with $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$, so $\beta_nL = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots$ and $f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi$, in the ratios $1 : 2.756 : 5.404$, off the lines.[^fr19a]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="glockenspiel">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A glockenspiel bar on two supports, swinging in its first three modes"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bar's partials at 1, 2.76 and 5.40 times its lowest frequency, off the whole-number lines"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A bar tuned to C6, 1047 Hz, struck a little off its middle. Computed: the stem positions. Illustrative: the starting strengths and the fading times. The bar is drawn on its two supports, at its fundamental's still points.</p>
</div></div>
```

The supports hold the drifts, and they sit at the fundamental's two still points, $0.224L$ from each end, so they barely damp the fundamental.[^ubc1] Xylophone and marimba bars are thinned underneath to put their first overtone on a whole-number line, 3× on a xylophone and 4× on a marimba; glockenspiel bars are left uniform.[^fr19b] The player sets the loudness by the strength of the blow, the brightness by the mallet, metal brighter and rubber warmer,[^mallet] and, by where the mallet lands, how strongly each mode starts. A table glockenspiel has no dampers, so players stop a note with a hand; one on a stand usually has a damper pedal.[^vsl]

Of post 2's conditions, the drifts break *$A$ is positive*: here $A$ is only $\geq 0$.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

It is the kalimba tine's beam equation, from the same slice of bar (fold above). Only the ends differ: on soft supports both ends are free, so at each end no bending moment and no shear force act, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. The supports are taken as not holding the bar at all; resting at the fundamental's still points, they are where that mode does not move.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses a 2×2 determinant</span></summary>

With $\lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4$, $X = b_1\cos\beta x + b_2\sin\beta x + b_3\cosh\beta x + b_4\sinh\beta x$. The free left end, $X''(0) = X'''(0) = 0$, gives $b_3 = b_1$ and $b_4 = b_2$. With $c_1, s_1, c_2, s_2$ as in the kalimba's fold, the free right end gives $(c_2 - c_1)b_1 + (s_2 - s_1)b_2 = 0$ and $(s_2 + s_1)b_1 + (c_2 - c_1)b_2 = 0$, whose determinant is $(c_2 - c_1)^2 - (s_2^2 - s_1^2) = 2 - 2c_1c_2$. So $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$, with roots $\beta L = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots$ For $\lambda = 0$, $X'''' = 0$ with free ends leaves exactly $X = a + bx$: two eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 0, whose coordinates move as $q = a + bt$. The fundamental's still points, where $X_1 = 0$, are at $0.224L$ and $0.776L$ (computed).

</details>
:::

## Drums {#drums}

A bass drum booms with no clear pitch; a kettledrum, one of the timpani, plays a note. Both heads are a sheet pulled tight, a string with a second dimension, and on the ideal head the frequencies fall between the lines. What separates the two drums is where each is struck, what surrounds its head, and which modes fade first; the step-through below takes these one at a time.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ on the disk } r < a, \\
u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim } r = a, \\
u(\cdot, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(\cdot, 0) = v_0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $c^2 = T/\sigma$, the tension per unit length of cut over the mass per unit area; $\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}$ is the [Laplacian](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#laplacian); and $v_0$ is the stick's blow, concentrated near the strike point.

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_{m,n} = c^2j_{m,n}^2/a^2$, where $j_{m,n}$ is the $n$-th positive zero of the [Bessel function](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bessel) $J_m$; the mode $J_m(j_{m,n}r/a)\cos m\theta$ has $m$ still lines through the center and $n - 1$ still circles inside the rim. So $f_{m,n} = c\,j_{m,n}/2\pi a$, in the ratios $1 : 1.593 : 2.136 : 2.295 : 2.653 : 2.917 : \cdots$, between the lines.[^fr3]

The bass drum is struck slightly off center, where it starts mostly round modes, off the lines and fading fast; the player shortens it by muffling the head with a leg or a towel.[^aleo] The kettledrum is struck between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, where the lowest round mode starts more weakly than the spoke modes. The air its head drags along pulls the spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base, and the round modes radiate their energy away within a fraction of a second.[^hpt1] The note is named at the (1,1) mode, its principal tone, and the modes above sit a fifth, an octave and a major tenth higher, the ratios 3/2, 2 and 5/2.[^hpt2] The timpanist retunes it by changing the head's tension, usually with a pedal; Viennese timpani use a hand lever.[^hpt3] A bass drum has a head at each end, commonly tuned about a fourth apart.[^hpb]

The ideal head keeps all six of post 2's conditions. The kettledrum's radiation breaks the symmetry condition, through the air around the head rather than at the ends ([above](#recipe)).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area and the divergence theorem</span></summary>

Let $\sigma$ be the head's mass per unit area. A small patch $D$ has mass $\iint_D\sigma\,dA$, so Newton's law for its up-and-down motion reads $\iint_D\sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA$ = the net upward force. A drumhead is a [membrane](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#membrane): a sheet with no stiffness of its own, stretched with the same tension $T$ in every direction, so across each short piece $ds$ of the patch's edge the sheet outside pulls with the force $T\,ds$, along the surface and outward. For small slopes the upward part of that pull is $T$ times the slope outward across the edge, $T\,\partial_nu\,ds$. Adding these around the edge turns, by the [divergence theorem](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#divergence-theorem), into adding $T\,\Delta u$ over the patch:
$$
T\oint_{\partial D}\partial_nu\,ds = T\iint_D\Delta u\,dA .
$$
This holds for every patch, however small, so $\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u$ at every point. In one dimension the same step is $u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx$, the string's. The rim is clamped to the shell: $u = 0$ there. The model leaves out bending stiffness, damping and the air on both sides of the head.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses polar coordinates</span></summary>

Write $\lambda = c^2k^2$, so a mode satisfies $-\Delta X = k^2X$ with $X = 0$ on the rim. In polar coordinates $\Delta X = X_{rr} + X_r/r + X_{\theta\theta}/r^2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator#Two_dimensions)). Substituting $X = R(r)\Theta(\theta)$ and multiplying by $r^2/R\Theta$ separates the equation, a [separation of variables](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#separation-of-variables): $(r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R)/R = -\Theta''/\Theta$, the left side depending only on $r$ and the right only on $\theta$, so both equal one constant. Going once around must bring $\Theta$ back to itself, so $\Theta = \cos m\theta$ or $\sin m\theta$ with $m = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, and the constant is $m^2$. Then $r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0$, Bessel's equation, whose solution finite at the center is $J_m(kr)$. The rim needs $J_m(ka) = 0$, so $k = j_{m,n}/a$. These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in $\theta$ reduces it to Bessel's equation term by term. Each frequency with $m \ge 1$ belongs to exactly two modes, the cosine and the sine, because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders share no positive zero (Bourget's conjecture, proved by C. L. Siegel, "Über einige Anwendungen diophantischer Approximationen", *Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Physikalisch-mathematische Klasse* (1929), no. 1; English translation by C. Fuchs, [*On Some Applications of Diophantine Approximations*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-88-7642-520-2), ed. U. Zannier, Edizioni della Normale, 2014).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The step-through's toy model <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area</span></summary>

*The strike.* A brief push at the point $p$ gives mode $i$ a starting speed in proportion to $X_i(p)$; divided by $(\iint X_i^2\,dA)^{1/2}$, on a head of radius 1 this weight is 1.09 at the center, 0.73 halfway out and 0.37 three-quarters out for the lowest round mode (0,1), and between 0.74 and 1.19 for the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) anywhere from halfway to three-quarters. A concert bass drum is played slightly off center (A. Graham, ["Proper Playing Areas"](https://theinstrumentalist.com/september-2017/proper-playing-areas/), *The Instrumentalist*, September 2017; ["How to play the bass drum properly"](https://www.interlochen.org/stories/how-to-play-bass-drum-properly), with Keith Aleo, Interlochen Center for the Arts, 2023), where the spoke modes move little.

*The air's mass.* Treat the air on both sides as not squeezable, and each mode locally as a ripple of wavenumber $k = j_{m,n}/a$. The air such a ripple moves reaches about $1/k$ from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about $2\rho/k$ per unit area ($\rho \approx 1.2$ kg/m³) to the head's $\sigma$: $\omega^2 = Tk^2/(\sigma + 2\rho/k)$, so coarse shapes slow down most, an [added mass](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#added-mass). With $\sigma \approx 0.26$ kg/m² and $a = 0.33$ m (T. A. Packer, [*Acoustics of the Orchestral Kettledrum*](https://etheses.durham.ac.uk/id/eprint/5633/), master's thesis, University of Durham, 1993, appendix B), $2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0$, and the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from $1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98$ to $1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24$, halfway to $1.5 : 2 : 2.5$; a full calculation of the air inside and around the head gets the rest (R. S. Christian, R. E. Davis, A. Tubis, C. A. Anderson, R. I. Mills and T. D. Rossing, ["Effects of air loading on timpani membrane vibrations"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.391449), *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 76 (1984), 1336–1345).

*The kettle.* The nearly sealed kettle acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, $V = \iint u\,dA$, adding $\tfrac12\eta V^2$ to the stored energy. Every mode with $m \ge 1$ sweeps no volume, since $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0$, so it keeps its frequency exactly; only the round modes are raised.

*What is left out.* Radiation, which takes the real kettledrum outside the theorem of this page's opening; the bass drum's second head, coupled to the first through the air in the shell; the fading, taken from measurement (Fletcher and Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), chapter 18).

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the drum →](drum.qmd)**

## A violin, bowed {#violin}

A bowed violin string holds a steady note with its partials exactly on the whole-number lines. It is post 2's string, kept going by the bow: the bow hair's friction carries the string along, then lets it slip back when the string's pull wins, and the string settles into one repeating cycle.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
As in post 2, $c^2 = T/\mu$. The bow's force depends on the slipping speed, not in proportion to it.

**The resonator's spectrum** is post 2's: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$ and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nc/2L$, on every line.

**The sound** is [Helmholtz motion](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#helmholtz-motion): two straight pieces joined by a corner that races from the nut to the bridge and back once per period, $2L/c$.[^fr10] So the playing frequency is $f_1$, the partials sit at $nf_1$, and partial $n$ pushes the bridge in proportion to $1/n$ (fold); the body changes their heights, not their positions.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="violin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A bowed string: two straight pieces joined by a corner that races between the nut and the bridge"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bowed sound's partials on every whole-number line, with the string's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">Helmholtz motion of an open G string, 196 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, computed for the ideal string, with strength 1/n, without the wooden body. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the string's modes, on every line too. The picture is the sum of the first 40 modes; dashed, the corner's path, two arcs of a parabola.</p>
</div></div>
```

Helmholtz watched this motion through a vibration microscope by 1860.[^helm] The model's cycle repeats exactly; a real bowed string is "nearly exactly periodic", and the bow locks the partials onto the lines although a real string's own modes run slightly sharp.[^wolfebow1] The left hand chooses $L$ by stopping the string, and adds vibrato; the bow's speed and its distance from the bridge set the loudness, the bow's force and nearness to the bridge the brightness, and the stroke the length.[^wolfebow2]

The string keeps all six of post 2's conditions; the bow breaks *linear* and feeds energy in.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Post 2 derives it ([section 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#newton)): on a short piece of string under tension $T$, the upward part of each end's pull is $T$ times the slope for small slopes, so the net force is $T\,u_{xx}\,dx$ and $\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}$; the nut and the bridge hold the ends still, $u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0$. The bow adds a force at one point, which depends on the motion there; how bow and string lock together is observed and modelled numerically (M. E. McIntyre, R. T. Schumacher and J. Woodhouse, ["On the oscillations of musical instruments"](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/mem2/papers/MUS-ACOUST/), *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 74 (1983), 1325–1345), and this page does not derive it.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Helmholtz motion as a sum of modes <span class="needs">uses the plucked-string formula of post 2</span></summary>

A vibration microscope's lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. With one, Helmholtz saw that at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at $x_c$. He showed that the corner's height is proportional to $x_c(L - x_c)$, so it traces two arcs of a parabola, and that the corner moves at the wave speed $c = 2Lf_1$. Put that height in place of the pluck's height $h$ in post 2's coefficients $B_n \propto h\sin(n\pi x_c/L)/(n^2x_c(L - x_c))$: the factor $x_c(L - x_c)$ cancels, leaving $\sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2$, and with $x_c = 2Lf_1t$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
u(x, t) = {} & \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} \\
& \times \sin(2\pi nf_1t)
\end{aligned}
$$
for some overall size $a$ (on the way back, $L < x_c < 2L$, the same formula describes a corner at $2L - x_c$ with negative height). The motion repeats exactly every $1/f_1$ seconds. The force on the bridge is $T$ times the slope there, and the slope of $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ carries the factor $n\pi/L$, so partial $n$ pushes the bridge in proportion to $1/n$.

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the violin →](violin.qmd)**

## A flute {#flute}

A flute plays a steady note on the lines. Close every hole and blow an ever faster, narrower airstream, and it sounds the tube's modes in turn, 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest: the open tube's spectrum, heard as the harmonic series.[^wolfefl1] The flute is a tube of air open at both ends, blown by a jet of air across the embouchure hole near one end, with no reed.
$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
p(0, t) = p(L, t) = 0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $p$ is the pressure minus room pressure and $c = \sqrt{K/\rho} \approx 343$ m/s the speed of sound ($K$ the air's [bulk modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bulk-modulus), $\rho$ its density); an open end holds room pressure, up to a small [end correction](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#end-correction). The drive is the jet, which the air's own back-and-forth motion at the hole swings into and out of the tube, adding air in step with the oscillation.[^fr16]

**The resonator's spectrum** has the string's numbers: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$ and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nc/2L$, on every line.[^pipes1]

**The sound** is one repeating cycle near the sounding mode, with partials at exact whole-number multiples; the jet's waveform and the tube decide which are strong.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="flute">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube open at both ends, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The flute's partials on every whole-number line, with the open tube's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D4, 294 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, all on the lines; their strengths, 1/n², are an illustrative choice. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the open tube's modes, on every line too. Picture: the air in the tube, darker where the pressure is higher, with thin slabs of air that bunch where it is squeezed.</p>
</div></div>
```

The player chooses $L$ with the keys, the loudness with the breath, and the register with that faster, narrower airstream, which jumps the tube to its next mode.[^wolfefl2]

In this model the air column keeps all six of post 2's conditions; the jet breaks *linear*.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives, including mixed ones</span></summary>

Let $\xi(x, t)$ be how far the air that normally sits at $x$ has moved along the tube, of cross-section $S$. The slab between $x$ and $x + dx$ has mass $\rho S\,dx$ and is pushed by the pressure difference across it, $S[p(x) - p(x + dx)] \approx -S\,p_x\,dx$, so $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$. Squeezed air pushes back: the slab is stretched by the fraction $\xi_x$, and for small changes its pressure drops in proportion, $p = -K\xi_x$, with $K$ the bulk modulus (about 1.4 times atmospheric pressure, for squeezing too fast for heat to flow). Together, $\xi_{tt} = c^2\xi_{xx}$ with $c^2 = K/\rho$; differentiating in $x$ and multiplying by $-K$ gives $p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx}$. At an open end the air meets the room, so $p = 0$; the air just outside moves with the air inside, so the tube acts slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius at each open end, the end correction (J. Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html), UNSW). The model takes a narrow, frictionless, cylindrical tube.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step</summary>

With $\lambda = c^2k^2$, a mode solves $X'' = -k^2X$, so $X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx$. Room pressure at $x = 0$ forces $a = 0$, and at $x = L$ needs $\sin kL = 0$, so $k = n\pi/L$: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$, $f_n = nc/2L$, the string's spectrum, with modes $\sin(n\pi x/L)$.

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the flute and the clarinet →](clarinet.qmd)**

## A clarinet {#clarinet}

A clarinet sounds a hollow note, nearly an octave below a flute of the same length.[^ovc1] The reason is the reed end: the tube is closed there and open at the bell, which halves its lowest frequency and leaves only odd multiples of it. The reed is a valve that keeps the air swinging.
$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
p_x(0, t) = 0 \ \text{(reed)}, \\ p(L, t) = 0 \ \text{(bell)}.
\end{gathered}
$$
The reed opens as the mouthpiece pressure rises and closes as it drops, so the air column controls the flow that feeds it.[^fr15] At the nearly shut reed the air cannot move, so it feels no net push: $p_x = 0$, a [Neumann condition](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#neumann). The letters $p$ and $c$ are the flute's.

**The resonator's spectrum.** $\lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2$ and $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$: only odd multiples of $c/4L$, half the flute's $c/2L$ for the same length.[^pipes2]

**The sound** is one repeating cycle near a resonance, with partials at every whole-number multiple; in the low register the tube makes the odd ones strong and the even ones weak, not absent.[^wolfecl1]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="clarinet">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube closed at the reed on the left and open at the bell, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The clarinet's partials on every whole-number line, strong odd ones and faint even ones, with the tube's own frequencies marked under the axis on the odd lines only"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D3, 147 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, on every line, strong odd and faint even ones; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice after Wolfe's description. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the tube's modes, on the odd lines only. Picture: the air column, closed at the reed on the left, drawn with the odd partials only; the faint even ones are left out of the picture.</p>
</div></div>
```

The tube's next mode is 3 times its lowest, so a clarinet overblows a twelfth, an octave and a fifth, where a flute overblows an octave; clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart.[^wolfecl2] The fingers choose $L$, the breath the loudness and brightness (harder is brighter), and the register key jumps the tube to its next mode.[^wolfecl3]

In this model the air column keeps all six of post 2's conditions; the reed breaks *linear*.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

The flute's derivation (fold above) gives $p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx}$ and $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$. At the reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move: $\xi = 0$ at all times, so $\xi_{tt} = 0$, and Newton's law $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$ gives $p_x = 0$. The bell is open: $p = 0$. A real clarinet's bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers, not the picture.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step</summary>

With $X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx$, the reed's $X'(0) = bk = 0$ forces $b = 0$, and the bell's $X(L) = 0$ needs $\cos kL = 0$, so $kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2$: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. So $\lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2$ and $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$, with modes $\cos\big((2n - 1)\pi x/2L\big)$.

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the clarinet →](clarinet.qmd)**

## A harmonica {#harmonica}

A harmonica reed's own overtones sit far off the lines, at 6.27 times its lowest frequency, yet the note it plays has partials only on the lines, odd and even both strong.[^pykett1] The reason is that you hear the air, not the reed. The reed, a small brass bar riveted at one end over a slot, swings through the slot, and lets through one identical puff of air per cycle; the sound comes mainly from the puffs.[^pykett2] It is the kalimba tine's problem, driven by airflow:
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_x = 0 \ \text{ at the rivet}, \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at the tip}.
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2 = Eh^2/12\rho$ for a reed of thickness $h$. The drive is the airflow through the slot, which the reed opens and shuts as it swings through, a [free reed](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#free-reed).

**The resonator's spectrum** is the tine's: $f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi$, ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, off the lines.

**The sound.** The reed settles into one repeating cycle, somewhat below its lowest mode's frequency,[^cott] so the puffs repeat, and repeating puffs have partials only at whole-number multiples. Each puff's shape, with the player's mouth and the reed chamber, decides which are strong, not the reed's own modes.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="harmonica">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A reed riveted over its slot, swinging through it and letting out one puff of air per cycle, with a trace of the airflow"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The blown reed's partials on every whole-number line, with the reed's own frequencies marked under the axis at 1 and 6.27 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A C5 reed, 523 Hz, blown. Stems: the sound's partials, at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, computed from the puff drawn on the right: one puff per cycle, open for about 30% of it, a shape chosen for illustration. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the reed's modes, at 1 and 6.27 times its lowest; the playing frequency sits somewhat below the lowest, drawn here at 1. The reed is drawn in its first mode, and the slot is drawn open only while the tip is above the plate.</p>
</div></div>
```

The breath sets the loudness and, through each puff's shape, the tone, while the pitch hardly moves.[^pykett3] Players bend notes down on a diatonic harmonica by reshaping mouth and throat; the bent note lies between the hole's two notes, because the hole's blow and draw reeds, over one chamber, both take part.[^bahnson]

The reed keeps all six of post 2's conditions; the valve breaks *linear*.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

It is the kalimba tine's beam equation (fold in the kalimba entry), for brass: clamped at the rivet, $u = u_x = 0$, and free at the tip, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. For a rectangular reed of width $w$ and thickness $h$, $I = wh^3/12$ and $S = wh$, so $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S = Eh^2/12\rho$, and $f_1 = (1.8751)^2\,h\sqrt{E/12\rho}/(2\pi L^2)$: the width cancels.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Why a repeating airflow has only whole-number partials, and how the demo makes its sound</summary>

Let $q(t)$ be the airflow through the slot. In the steady oscillation it repeats every $P = 1/f_p$ seconds, $q(t + P) = q(t)$, so its [Fourier series](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#fourier-series) contains only $\cos(2\pi nt/P)$ and $\sin(2\pi nt/P)$: frequencies $nf_p$ ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)). The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up. That the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds, but not derived here; a plausible picture is that the airflow feeds mainly the first mode, and the others move only as they are pushed, at multiples of $f_p$. The demo's puff is $q = \max(0, \sin 2\pi f_pt - 0.6)$, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short; its Fourier coefficients, with a gentle roll-off, are the stems.

</details>
:::

**[Deep dive: the harmonica →](harmonica.qmd)**

## A theremin {#theremin}

A theremin is played without being touched, and its tone glides as the hand moves.[^thm1] It makes the tone with electric circuits, each a coil and a capacitor, an [LC circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LC_circuit), whose charge swings like a mass on a spring:
$$
\ddot q = -\frac{1}{LC}\,q .
$$
Here $q$ is the charge on the capacitor, $L$ the coil's [inductance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#inductance) and $C$ the [capacitance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#capacitance), so $A = 1/LC$, one number. The drive is an amplifier that feeds the circuit in step with its swing and limits it to a steady size.[^osc]

**The resonator's spectrum.** One eigenvalue, $\lambda = 1/LC$, so one frequency, $f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, a radio frequency below 500 kHz.[^thm2]

**The sound.** The instrument runs two such circuits, one fixed and one whose capacitance the player's hand changes, and a mixer outputs the difference of their frequencies, in the audible range ([heterodyning](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#heterodyning)). The demo plays a sine theremin: one partial.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="theremin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A coil and a capacitor, with the charge sloshing between the capacitor's plates"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="One partial, at 1 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">An idealized sine theremin at A4, 440 Hz: one stem. A real theremin's tone is not a pure sine: it has overtones. No resonator ticks: the circuits' own frequencies are radio frequencies, far beyond this ruler, and the tone you hear is the difference of two of them. Picture: one coil-and-capacitor circuit, its charge sloshing between the plates, slowed to about one swing a second.</p>
</div></div>
```

A real theremin's tone is not a pure sine. Most players set the pitch with the right hand's distance from one antenna and the loudness with the left hand's distance from the other. Leon Theremin invented the instrument in 1920 and patented it in 1928.[^thm3]

The circuit alone keeps all six of post 2's conditions; the amplifier breaks *linear*, and a moving hand changes $C$ as the circuit swings, breaking *unchanging in time*, like post 2's turned peg.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Kirchhoff's voltage law, which balances voltages as Newton's law balances forces, says that the voltages around a closed loop add to zero. A capacitor holding charge $q$ has the voltage $q/C$ across it; a coil carrying the current $I = \dot q$ has the voltage $L\,\dot I$. Around the loop, $L\,\ddot q + q/C = 0$, that is, $\ddot q = -q/LC$: the coil plays the mass and $1/C$ the spring's stiffness. For ideal parts both laws are linear, so no small-motion step is needed.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>How two radio frequencies make one audible tone</summary>

A mixer multiplies the two oscillators' signals, and $\sin(2\pi f_1t)\sin(2\pi f_2t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t)$; a filter keeps the difference. With both near a few hundred kilohertz, a hand that changes one circuit's capacitance by a small fraction moves the difference across the whole audible range. Real theremins' mixers and circuits add overtones, on the whole-number lines of the difference frequency, since the output repeats at that rate.

</details>
:::

[^wolfebow2]: J. Wolfe, [Articulation and vibrato on the violin](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/violinarticulation.html), UNSW: the left hand stops the string and adds vibrato; J. Wolfe, [The bowed string](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Bows.html), UNSW: bow speed, position and force.
[^wolfefl1]: J. Wolfe, [Flute acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/fluteacoustics.html), UNSW: open at both ends; the harmonic series with every hole closed.
[^fr16]: Fletcher and Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), chapter 16 (flutes); Wolfe, [Flute acoustics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/fluteacoustics.html): the jet.
[^pipes1]: J. Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html), UNSW: open and closed ends; [Fletcher and Rossing](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), chapter 8 (pipes).
[^wolfefl2]: Wolfe, [Flute acoustics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/fluteacoustics.html): registers.
[^ovc1]: J. Wolfe, [Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets)](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/flutes.v.clarinets.html), UNSW: a clarinet about an octave below a flute of the same length.
[^fr15]: Fletcher and Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), chapter 15 (woodwind reed instruments).
[^pipes2]: Wolfe, [Pipes and harmonics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/pipes.html): a pipe closed at one end.
[^wolfecl1]: J. Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics: an introduction](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html), UNSW: strong odd harmonics in the low register.
[^wolfecl2]: Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html): the register key and the twelfth; Wolfe, [Open vs closed pipes](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/flutes.v.clarinets.html): overblowing a twelfth.
[^wolfecl3]: Wolfe, [Clarinet acoustics](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/clarinetacoustics.html): louder playing is brighter; the register key.
[^pykett1]: C. Pykett, [The physics of free reeds](https://colinpykett.org.uk/physics-of-free-reed-wind-instruments.htm), 2023: odd and even harmonics.
[^pykett2]: Pykett, [The physics of free reeds](https://colinpykett.org.uk/physics-of-free-reed-wind-instruments.htm): the sound comes from the puffs.
[^cott]: J. Cottingham, [Acoustics of free-reed instruments](https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/acoustics-of-free-reed-instruments), *Physics Today* 64(3), 2011, 44–48 ([doi:10.1063/1.3563819](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3563819)), p. 45: the playing frequency below the reed's own.
[^pykett3]: Pykett, [The physics of free reeds](https://colinpykett.org.uk/physics-of-free-reed-wind-instruments.htm): pitch nearly independent of wind pressure, which changes loudness and puff shape.
[^bahnson]: H. T. Bahnson, J. F. Antaki and Q. C. Beery, ["Acoustical and physical dynamics of the diatonic harmonica"](https://www.cs.bu.edu/fac/snyder/TablatureWeb/Bahnson%20JASA%201998.pdf), *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 103 (1998), 2134–2144; Cottingham, [Acoustics of free-reed instruments](https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/acoustics-of-free-reed-instruments), on bending.
[^thm1]: Wikipedia, [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin).
[^osc]: Wikipedia, [Electronic oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_oscillator): an amplifier feeding a tuned circuit in phase, its amplitude limited by a nonlinearity.
[^thm2]: Wikipedia, [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin): two radio-frequency oscillators below 500 kHz.
[^thm3]: Wikipedia, [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin): the hands; invented 1920, patented 1928.

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
// One drumhead, two drums: a five-step toy model (bass drum above, timpani below).
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = window.Core;
  var J11 = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.m === 1 && d.n === 1; })[0].j, J01 = C.DR[0].j;
  var MODES = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.j / J11 <= 3.6; });
  function kind(d) { return d.m === 0 ? "round" : d.n === 1 ? "spoke" : "other"; }
  var COL = { round: "--pos", spoke: "--neg", other: "--metal" };
  var STEPS = {
    1: ["Same head, same operator", "Both drums start as this entry's operator on a disk with the rim held still. On this ideal head the frequencies fall off the dashed lines, and the two diagrams are identical. Two kinds of mode will matter: the round modes, with no line through the center, and the spoke modes, with lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim."],
    2: ["Where you strike decides which modes start", "A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. A bass drum is struck slightly off center, where the spoke modes barely move, so its lowest modes are mostly round ones. A kettledrum is struck between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, where the lowest round mode starts more weakly than the spoke modes."],
    3: ["The air adds mass, most to coarse shapes", "Air on both sides of the head moves with it. A ripple of wavenumber k drags along a layer of air about 1/k thick, so a coarse mode carries more extra mass and slows down more: f ∝ k / √(σ + 2ρ/k). This happens to both drums. It stretches the spoke modes toward the dashed lines; in this toy model it gets about halfway, and a full calculation of the air gets the rest."],
    4: ["What surrounds each head", "A kettledrum's bowl is nearly sealed, so its air resists only shapes that change the volume it encloses. A mode with lines through the center pushes up as much as it pulls down, sweeps no net volume, and keeps its frequency exactly; only the round modes are raised. A bass drum has no kettle: its second head, coupled through the air in the shell, splits its lowest modes instead (not modelled here)."],
    5: ["What fades", "A round mode pumps air like a piston and radiates its energy away within a fraction of a second. On the bass drum, a strike near the center starts mostly round modes among the lowest ones. How long the rest rings is the player's choice: a leg or a towel on the head muffles every mode under it, for short, dry notes (press Muffle); lift it and the drum rings on. The leftover stems that land near a line are chance near-misses of this toy model, not a set of modes pulled onto the lines, and a real bass drum's second head, coupled through the air in its shell, splits its lowest modes, which the model leaves out. The result is a boom with no clear pitch, as intended. On the kettledrum the spoke modes ring on, near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base an octave below the (1,1): a note. Real timpani sit closer to the lines than this toy model; press Measured ratios to see and hear them."]
  };
  var step = 1, rT = 0.62, MU = 3.03, KK = 1, RB = 0.15, MUFFLE = false;
  var drums = {
    bass: { kettle: false, spec: document.getElementById("tdSb"), head: document.getElementById("tdHb"), verdict: document.getElementById("tdVb"), disp: null },
    timp: { kettle: true, spec: document.getElementById("tdSt"), head: document.getElementById("tdHt"), verdict: document.getElementById("tdVt"), disp: null }
  };
  function rOf(D) { return D === drums.timp ? rT : RB; }
  // frequency of mode d with air loading mu and kettle kk (relative units)
  function omega(d, mu, kk) { var lam = d.j * d.j + (d.m === 0 ? kk * Math.pow(J01, 4) / (d.j * d.j) : 0); return Math.sqrt(lam / (1 + mu / d.j)); }
  function excite(d, r) { return Math.abs(C.J(d.m, d.j * r)) / Math.sqrt(d.norm); }
  function target(D) {
    var mu = step >= 3 ? MU : 0, kk = step >= 4 && D.kettle ? KK : 0, r = rOf(D);
    var w11 = omega({ m: 1, j: J11 }, mu, 0), hs = MODES.map(function (d) { return step >= 2 ? excite(d, r) : 1; }), hm = Math.max.apply(null, hs);
    // step 5: round modes radiate away; Muffle (bass drum only) damps every mode under the player's leg or towel, at any step
    return MODES.map(function (d, i) {
      var x = 2 * omega(d, mu, kk) / w11;
      if (D === drums.timp && MEASURED && d.n === 1 && d.m >= 1) x = d.m + 1; // the measured pattern, not this model
      return { x: x, h: hs[i] / hm, gone: (step >= 5 && d.m === 0) || (D === drums.bass && MUFFLE), d: d };
    });
  }
  var XMIN = 0.8, XMAX = 7;
  function drawSpec(D) {
    var cv = D.spec, dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var L = 8, R = W - 8, base = H - 22, top = 10;
    function X(x) { return L + (R - L) * (x - XMIN) / (XMAX - XMIN); }
    g.font = "12px IBM Plex Mono, ui-monospace, monospace"; g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted");
    [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].forEach(function (x) { g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); g.setLineDash([4, 4]); g.lineWidth = 1; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(x), top); g.lineTo(X(x), base); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]); g.fillText(x + "×", X(x), base + 16); });
    g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(L, base); g.lineTo(R, base); g.stroke();
    D.disp.forEach(function (p) {
      if (p.x < XMIN || p.x > XMAX || p.h < 0.01) return;
      var hh = (base - top) * p.h;
      g.strokeStyle = C.rgb(COL[kind(p.d)]); g.lineWidth = W < 420 ? 3 : 4; g.lineCap = "round";
      if (p.gone > 0.5) { g.lineWidth = 1.5; g.setLineDash([3, 3]); }
      g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(p.x), base); g.lineTo(X(p.x), base - hh); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]);
    });
  }
  function drawHead(D) {
    var cv = D.head, dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = Math.min(W, H) / 2 - 6, r = rOf(D);
    g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--paper"); g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.lineWidth = 2; g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill(); g.stroke();
    if (D.kettle) { g.setLineDash([3, 3]); g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R * 0.9, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]); }
    if (step >= 2) {
      g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx + r * R, cy, 5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill();
      g.font = "11px IBM Plex Sans Condensed, system-ui, sans-serif"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); if (r < 0.4) { g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillText("strike", cx + r * R, cy - 9); } else { g.textAlign = "right"; g.fillText("strike", cx + r * R - 8, cy + 4); }
    }
  }
  var GAL = MODES.slice(0, 10);
  function drawGallery() {
    var cv = document.getElementById("tdGal"), dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var n = W < 420 ? 5 : 10, rows = W < 420 ? 2 : 1, cw = W / n, rh = H / rows, R = Math.max(4, Math.min(cw, rh - 18) / 2 - 3), S = 2 * Math.ceil(R);
    var pr = C.col["--ink"], nr = C.col["--metal"];
    GAL.forEach(function (d, i) {
      var cx = (i % n) * cw + cw / 2, cy = Math.floor(i / n) * rh + R + 3, N = Math.round(S * dpr), img = g.createImageData(N, N);
      for (var py = 0; py < N; py++) for (var px = 0; px < N; px++) {
        var x = (px + 0.5) / N * 2 - 1, y = (py + 0.5) / N * 2 - 1, rr = Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y), o = 4 * (py * N + px);
        if (rr > 1) { img.data[o + 3] = 0; continue; }
        var v = C.J(d.m, d.j * rr) * Math.cos(d.m * Math.atan2(y, x)), c = v >= 0 ? pr : nr, a = Math.min(1, Math.abs(v) * 2.6);
        img.data[o] = c[0]; img.data[o + 1] = c[1]; img.data[o + 2] = c[2]; img.data[o + 3] = Math.round(40 + 215 * a);
      }
      var off = document.createElement("canvas"); off.width = N; off.height = N; off.getContext("2d").putImageData(img, 0, 0);
      g.save(); g.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0); g.drawImage(off, Math.round((cx - S / 2) * dpr), Math.round((cy - S / 2) * dpr)); g.restore();
      g.strokeStyle = C.rgb(COL[kind(d)]); g.lineWidth = 2.5; g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R + 1.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.stroke();
      g.font = "12px IBM Plex Mono, ui-monospace, monospace"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillText("(" + d.m + "," + d.n + ")", cx, cy + R + 15);
    });
  }
  function verdict(D) {
    if (step < 2) return "";
    var live = D.disp.filter(function (p) { return p.h > 0.15 && !(p.gone > 0.5) && p.x <= XMAX; }).sort(function (a, b) { return b.h - a.h; }).slice(0, 5).sort(function (a, b) { return a.x - b.x; });
    if (!live.length) return D === drums.bass && MUFFLE ? "muffled: a short note" : "everything fades fast";
    return "tallest stems at " + live.map(function (p) { return p.x.toFixed(2) + "×"; }).join(" · ");
  }
  var anim = 0;
  function render() {
    var done = true;
    ["bass", "timp"].forEach(function (k) {
      var D = drums[k], T = target(D);
      if (!D.disp) D.disp = T.map(function (p) { return { x: p.x, h: p.h, gone: p.gone ? 1 : 0, d: p.d }; });
      D.disp.forEach(function (p, i) {
        var q = T[i], gx = q.x - p.x, gh = q.h - p.h, gg = (q.gone ? 1 : 0) - p.gone;
        p.x += 0.18 * gx; p.h += 0.18 * gh; p.gone += 0.18 * gg;
        if (Math.abs(gx) > 1e-3 || Math.abs(gh) > 1e-3 || Math.abs(gg) > 1e-3) done = false; else { p.x = q.x; p.h = q.h; p.gone = q.gone ? 1 : 0; }
      });
      drawSpec(D); drawHead(D); D.verdict.textContent = verdict(D);
    });
    anim = done ? 0 : requestAnimationFrame(render);
  }
  function kick() { if (!anim) anim = requestAnimationFrame(render); }
  var btns = document.querySelectorAll("#td [data-td]");
  function setStep(s) {
    step = s;
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(btns, function (b) { b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", +b.getAttribute("data-td") === s ? "true" : "false"); });
    document.getElementById("tdT").textContent = s + " · " + STEPS[s][0];
    document.getElementById("tdX").textContent = STEPS[s][1];
    if (C.reduce) { drums.bass.disp = null; drums.timp.disp = null; }
    kick();
  }
  Array.prototype.forEach.call(btns, function (b) { b.addEventListener("click", function () { setStep(+b.getAttribute("data-td")); }); });
  // Sound: each drum at its own size. The bass drum's lowest round mode sits near 50 Hz; the timpani's (1,1) is set to 130.8 Hz (C3).
  // From step 5 the round modes die within a fraction of a second, as they radiate their energy away.
  var MEASURED = false;
  function parts(k) {
    var D = drums[k], T = target(D), mu = step >= 3 ? MU : 0;
    var ref = k === "bass" ? 50 / (2 * omega(C.DR[0], mu, 0) / omega({ m: 1, j: J11 }, mu, 0)) : 130.8 / 2;
    return T.map(function (p) {
      var x = p.x;
      return { f: ref * x, amp: p.h * (step >= 2 ? 1 : 0.5), tau: p.gone ? (k === "bass" ? 0.25 : 0.07) : 1.6 / (1 + 0.03 * x * x) };
    });
  }
  function play(k) { C.play(C.render(parts(k), 3.5), 0.8); }
  document.getElementById("tdPb").addEventListener("click", function () { play("bass"); });
  document.getElementById("tdPt").addEventListener("click", function () { play("timp"); });
  var mf = document.getElementById("tdMuf");
  mf.addEventListener("click", function () { MUFFLE = !MUFFLE; mf.setAttribute("aria-pressed", MUFFLE ? "true" : "false"); kick(); play("bass"); });
  var mb = document.getElementById("tdM");
  mb.addEventListener("click", function () { MEASURED = !MEASURED; mb.setAttribute("aria-pressed", MEASURED ? "true" : "false"); kick(); if (MEASURED) play("timp"); });
  function bind(id, fmt, set) {
    var el = document.getElementById(id), o = document.getElementById(id + "o");
    function upd() { set(+el.value); o.textContent = fmt(+el.value); kick(); }
    el.addEventListener("input", upd); o.textContent = fmt(+el.value);
  }
  bind("tdR", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { rT = v; });
  bind("tdMu", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { MU = v; });
  bind("tdK", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { KK = v; });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
  C.onTheme(function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
  setStep(1); drawGallery();
  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.ready) document.fonts.ready.then(function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
})();
</script>
<script src="orchestra.js"></script>
<script>
// The orchestra: one instrument from each Hornbostel–Sachs class, drawn and played by orchestra.js.
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var O = window.Orchestra; if (!O) return;
  // On this page each family's card points to its entry below.
  var HERE = { electro: "The theremin: entry below", chord: "The piano: entry below", aero: "The clarinet: entry below", idio: "The glockenspiel: entry below", membrane: "The two drums: entry below" };
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) { if (HERE[f.id]) f.where = HERE[f.id]; });
  var fams = document.getElementById("oFams"), mute = {};
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) {
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.className = "chip"; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", "true");
    b.style.setProperty("--c", "rgb(" + f.hue.join(",") + ")"); b.innerHTML = '<span class="dot"></span>' + f.inst;
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { mute[f.id] = !mute[f.id]; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", mute[f.id] ? "false" : "true"); applyMute(f.id); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
    fams.appendChild(b);
  });
  var cv = document.getElementById("oStage"), g = cv.getContext("2d"), timeEl = document.getElementById("oTime");
  var tlPerf = O.timeline(false), tlFull = O.timeline(true), cur = tlPerf, ctx = null, t0 = 0, raf = 0, fg = null;
  tlPerf.mute = mute; tlFull.mute = mute;
  var REST = O.beatToSec(8 * 16 + 4.15);
  function fit() {
    var full = document.fullscreenElement === cv, dpr = Math.min(2, window.devicePixelRatio || 1);
    var w = full ? Math.min(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight * 16 / 9) : cv.getBoundingClientRect().width;
    w = Math.max(320, Math.round(w * dpr)); cv.width = w; cv.height = Math.round(w * 9 / 16);
  }
  function drawRest() { O.drawAt(g, REST, cv.width, cv.height, tlPerf); }
  function mmss(x) { x = Math.max(0, Math.round(x)); return Math.floor(x / 60) + ":" + ("0" + x % 60).slice(-2); }
  function applyMute(id) { if (fg && ctx) fg[id].gain.setTargetAtTime(mute[id] ? 0 : 1, ctx.currentTime, 0.03); }
  function frame() {
    if (!ctx) return;
    var t = ctx.currentTime - t0;
    if (t > cur.dur) { stop(); return; }
    O.drawAt(g, Math.max(0, t), cv.width, cv.height, cur);
    timeEl.textContent = mmss(t) + " / " + mmss(cur.dur);
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  }
  function stop() {
    cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
    if (ctx) { try { ctx.close(); } catch (e) {} }
    ctx = null; fg = null; timeEl.textContent = "Ready"; drawRest();
  }
  function play(full) {
    stop(); cur = full ? tlFull : tlPerf;
    var AC = window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext;
    if (!AC) { timeEl.textContent = "This browser cannot play Web Audio."; return; }
    ctx = new AC(); if (ctx.resume) ctx.resume();
    var my = ctx; timeEl.textContent = "Computing the sounds…";
    setTimeout(function () {
      if (ctx !== my) return;
      var cache = O.prepare(ctx, cur.notes);
      t0 = ctx.currentTime + 0.2;
      fg = O.schedule(ctx, cur.notes, t0, { cache: cache, mute: mute });
      raf = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }, 30);
  }
  document.getElementById("oPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { play(false); });
  document.getElementById("oFull").addEventListener("click", function () { play(true); });
  document.getElementById("oStop").addEventListener("click", stop);
  var fsb = document.getElementById("oFs");
  if (!cv.requestFullscreen) fsb.hidden = true;
  fsb.addEventListener("click", function () { if (cv.requestFullscreen) cv.requestFullscreen().catch(function () {}); });
  document.addEventListener("fullscreenchange", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  fit(); drawRest();
  var faces = ['700 48px "LM Roman"', 'italic 24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Sans"', '24px "LM Math"'];
  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.load) Promise.all(faces.map(function (f) { return document.fonts.load(f, "A−κ♯"); })).then(function () { if (!ctx) drawRest(); }, function () {});
})();
</script>
```
